lessons.title: String Fundamentals And Manipulation
lessons.objective: Work with strings as arrays of characters, apply built-in and manual manipulation techniques correctly, and understand the complexity cost of common string operations.
concepts: Strings as immutable character sequences in most languages
Why string concatenation in a loop is O(n²) and how to fix it
Character access and ASCII values (a=97, A=65, 0=48)
String reversal using the two-pointer approach
Substring extraction cost: O(k) not O(1)
String comparison: O(n) in the worst case
StringBuilder / array join pattern for O(n) string construction
Common interview operations: reverse, palindrome check, character counting
lessons.explanation:
In JavaScript, strings are immutable sequences of characters. Every string operation that produces a new string allocates new memory.

This has a critical performance consequence: string concatenation with + in a loop is O(n²). Each iteration creates a new string by copying all existing characters plus the new one. After n iterations of appending one character, total copies = 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = O(n²).

The fix: collect characters in an array and join at the end. arr.push(char) is O(1) amortized, and arr.join('') is one O(n) pass. Total: O(n).

Every character has an ASCII value accessible via charCodeAt(): 'a' = 97, 'z' = 122, 'A' = 65, 'Z' = 90, '0' = 48, '9' = 57. Problems involving character counting, anagram detection, and frequency maps all rely on this.

String reversal using two pointers: convert to array (unavoidable — strings are immutable), swap left and right characters converging inward, join back. O(n) time, O(n) space for the array copy.
lessons.analogy: String concatenation in a loop is like hand-copying a growing manuscript. Each time you add a sentence, you copy the entire manuscript so far plus the new sentence onto fresh paper. After 1000 sentences you have copied roughly 500,000 sentences worth of text total. The array-join pattern is like writing sentences on separate index cards and then binding them once at the end — O(n) cards written, one O(n) binding step.

visual_explanation.description: Draw two columns. Left column: 'Loop with += operator'. Right column: 'Array push then join'. For the left column, show 5 iterations where each iteration creates a new string: '' → 'a' (copy 0), 'a' → 'ab' (copy 1), 'ab' → 'abc' (copy 2), 'abc' → 'abcd' (copy 3), 'abcd' → 'abcde' (copy 4). Total copies: 0+1+2+3+4 = 10 for n=5. Draw the formula: n(n-1)/2 = O(n²). For the right column: push push push push push (5 O(1) operations), then one join (O(n)). Total: O(n). Annotate the difference at n=1,000,000: left = 500 billion operations, right = 1 million operations.

code_example.explanation: The 26-element fixed array for letter counting is O(1) space because the array size is constant — not proportional to n. This is a common space optimisation in anagram and frequency problems. Using charCodeAt(0) - 97 converts 'a'→0, 'b'→1, ..., 'z'→25, giving a perfect index for a 26-element array.

common_mistakes: Concatenating strings in a loop with the + operator — always collect in an array and call join at the end. This single habit eliminates a class of hidden O(n²) algorithms
Treating strings as mutable — s[0] = 'x' silently fails in JavaScript (does nothing in non-strict mode). Convert to array first for any character modification
Forgetting that s.slice(l, r) is O(r-l) not O(1) — calling slice inside a loop creates O(n²) in the worst case. Prefer index arithmetic when possible

interview_war_story.story: The problem: reverse each word in a sentence while keeping word order. The candidate wrote a function that reversed each word using a loop with += concatenation. For n words each of length m, the total complexity was O(n × m²) — hidden quadratic inside each word reversal. The interviewer asked 'What is the complexity of reversing one word in your solution?' The candidate said 'O(m) — one loop.' The interviewer said 'Each += creates a new string copy.' The candidate immediately switched to the array-join pattern and fixed it to O(n × m). The candidate got the offer — not because they got it right the first time, but because they understood the correction immediately when prompted.
interview_war_story.lesson: String += inside any loop is O(n²). The fix is always the same: push to an array, join once at the end. Know this before walking into any interview.

lessons.interview_relevance: String manipulation is present in nearly every interview. The most common traps: hidden O(n²) from string concatenation, forgetting that substring is O(k) not O(1), and not knowing ASCII values for letter arithmetic. Demonstrating the array-join pattern and the 26-element fixed array signals professional string handling.

questions.question: A function builds a result string by concatenating n characters one at a time using +=. What is the total time complexity and why?
options: O(n) — one character is added per iteration
O(n²) — each += creates a NEW string by copying all previous characters plus the new one. After n iterations: 0+1+2+...+(n-1) = n(n-1)/2 total copies = O(n²)
O(n log n) — string operations are logarithmic
O(1) — JavaScript engines optimise string concatenation
questions.explanation: String immutability means += cannot append in-place. It creates a brand new string each time. The i-th iteration copies i characters. Total copies = 0+1+2+...+(n-1) = n(n-1)/2 = O(n²). The fix: push to an array (O(1) amortized per push), then join once (O(n)). Total: O(n).

questions.question: What is the ASCII value of 'c', and what index would it map to in a 26-element letter frequency array?
options: ASCII 67, index 3
ASCII 99, index 2
ASCII 99, index 3
ASCII 67, index 2
questions.explanation: 'c'.charCodeAt(0) = 99. Index = 99 - 97 = 2. 'a'=97→index 0, 'b'=98→index 1, 'c'=99→index 2. The formula is charCode - 97 for lowercase letters. This maps 'a' to 0 and 'z' to 25, fitting perfectly in a 26-element array.

questions.question: Why is calling s.slice(l, r) inside a loop O(n²) in the worst case?
options: slice uses binary search internally
slice creates a new string of length (r-l), copying those characters. Called n times in a loop with segments of length proportional to n, the total copies are O(n²)
slice is O(1) — it just returns a reference to part of the original string
slice is O(n log n) because it sorts the characters
questions.explanation: s.slice(l, r) copies r-l characters and returns a new string. It is O(r-l) per call, not O(1). If called n times in a loop with r-l proportional to n each time, total work is O(n²). Prefer tracking indices (l and r) and only extracting the slice when needed outside the loop.

coding_quest.title: Reverse Words In A Sentence
coding_quest.problem_statement: Given a string s containing words separated by spaces, reverse each individual word while keeping the word order the same. 'hello world' → 'olleh dlrow'. Implement two versions: one using string += (to see the O(n²) problem), and one using array join (the correct O(n) approach). The array join version must not use any built-in reverse method.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: VERSION 1 is shown deliberately — it produces correct output but has hidden O(m²) complexity per word reversal due to string +=. At small inputs this is invisible. At large inputs (reversing a 1000-character word 1000 times), the slow version processes 1 billion character copies while the fast version processes 1 million.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n × m²) where n=number of words, m=average word length

optimal_solution.complexity: O(n) total — each character visited and swapped at most once

hints.text: For each word: split it into an array of characters with word.split(''). Then use two pointers (left=0, right=chars.length-1). While left < right: swap chars[left] and chars[right], then advance left and retreat right. Finally: chars.join('') to get the reversed word.

The two-pointer swap: [chars[left], chars[right]] = [chars[right], chars[left]]. This is O(1) — just moving references, no string copying. Compare this to reversed += word[i] which copies an entire growing string each iteration.
const chars = word.split(''); let left = 0, right = chars.length - 1; while (left < right) { [chars[left], chars[right]] = [chars[right], chars[left]]; left++; right--; } result.push(chars.join(''));

lessons.mini_challenge: Write a function isAnagram(s, t) that returns true if t is an anagram of s without using sorting. First write a version using a hash map (O(n) space). Then write a version using a fixed 26-element array (O(1) space). State the time and space complexity of each.

theory_mcq.question: Why does building a string via repeated concatenation in a loop (`result += c`) become O(n²), even though it looks like a simple O(n) loop?
options: Because loops are always O(n²) in JavaScript

Because strings are immutable — each `+=` operation must allocate an entirely NEW string and copy all previously accumulated characters into it, so the total copying work across n iterations sums to 0+1+2+...+(n-1) = O(n²)
Because concatenation is a deprecated operation
It is actually O(n), not O(n²); the lesson's claim is incorrect
theory_mcq.explanation: Since strings can't be mutated in place, each concatenation creates a new string copy of everything accumulated so far PLUS the new character. Summed across n iterations, this produces a triangular-number total of copied characters, giving O(n²) overall despite the deceptively simple-looking loop.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the array-push-then-join pattern (`parts.push(c)` then `parts.join('')`) achieve O(n) total time, fixing the concatenation problem?
options: Because array push is always instant with zero cost

Because pushing to an array is O(1) amortized per operation (no copying of all previous content each time, unlike string concatenation), and the single final .join() call does one O(n) pass to build the final string — giving O(n) total instead of O(n²)
Because arrays and strings are identical data structures internally
This pattern is actually slower than direct concatenation
theory_mcq.explanation: Array push doesn't require copying all prior elements (it's amortized O(1), per L1's dynamic array lesson) — accumulating n elements this way is O(n) total. The final .join() does exactly one pass over all elements, O(n). Combined: O(n) + O(n) = O(n), versus the O(n²) of repeated string concatenation.

logic_mcq.question: In `countLetters`, why is `c.charCodeAt(0) - 97` used to compute the array index for a given lowercase character?
options: This is an arbitrary, meaningless calculation

Since 'a' has ASCII code 97, subtracting 97 from any lowercase letter's char code maps 'a'->0, 'b'->1, ..., 'z'->25, exactly matching the indices of a 26-element array representing each letter of the alphabet
It converts the character to uppercase
It always returns 0 regardless of the input character
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the ASCII arithmetic trick the lesson demonstrates: 'a'=97, so any lowercase letter's char code minus 97 gives its zero-indexed position in the alphabet (a=0, b=1, ..., z=25), which directly maps to indices in a 26-element frequency array without needing a hash map.

logic_mcq.question: What does `countLetters('aab')` return, tracing through the function?
options: [2,1,0,...,0] — index 0 ('a') is incremented twice (count=2), index 1 ('b') is incremented once (count=1), all other 24 indices remain 0
An error, since the function doesn't handle repeated characters
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact stated result: 'a' appears twice (incrementing index 0 to 2), 'b' appears once (incrementing index 1 to 1), and the remaining 24 letters of the alphabet are never encountered, staying at their initial value of 0.

syntax_mcq.question: What does `parts.join('')` do when `parts` is an array of single characters?
options: It sorts the array alphabetically
It concatenates all elements of the array into a single string, with no separator between them (since the join argument is an empty string), producing the final assembled string in one O(n) operation
It reverses the array
It returns the array unchanged as an array
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.join(separator)` concatenates all array elements into a single string, inserting the given separator between each pair. With an empty string `''` as the separator, elements are joined directly with nothing between them, producing a plain concatenated string.

syntax_mcq.question: In `s.split('')`, what does this expression do to a string `s`, and why is it necessary before reversing a string with the two-pointer pattern?
options: It deletes the string entirely

It converts the string into an array of individual characters; this is necessary because strings are immutable in JavaScript and cannot be modified in-place by swapping characters, so an array copy is required to perform in-place-style swaps
It capitalizes every character
It has no functional effect
syntax_mcq.explanation: Since JS strings can't be mutated character-by-character directly, `.split('')` creates a mutable array copy of the characters, on which the two-pointer swap technique (`[arr[left], arr[right]] = [arr[right], arr[left]]`) can actually operate, before rejoining into a final string.

lessons.title: Anagrams And Character Maps
lessons.objective: Solve anagram detection and grouping problems using character frequency maps, and extend the pattern to the sliding window for substring-level anagram search.
concepts: Anagram definition: same characters, same frequencies, any order
Character frequency map as the canonical anagram fingerprint
Comparing two frequency maps: O(1) for fixed alphabet
Group Anagrams: sorted key or frequency tuple as hash key
Sliding window anagram: find all anagram substrings of s in O(n)
Valid Anagram: O(n) with a frequency array
Character map vs sorting: O(n) vs O(n log n)
lessons.explanation:
Two strings are anagrams if and only if they have identical character frequencies. This converts anagram problems into frequency comparison problems.

A frequency map (or 26-element array) is the canonical fingerprint of a string for anagram purposes. Comparing two frequency maps takes O(26) = O(1) for fixed lowercase-alphabet input.

Valid Anagram: single pass through both strings, increment for s, decrement for t, check all zeros.

Group Anagrams: use the sorted string (or frequency tuple) as a hash map key — all anagrams produce the same key and map to the same group.

Find All Anagrams in a String: sliding window of size len(p) over s, comparing the window's frequency map to p's frequency map. Update the window map incrementally in O(1) per step. Total: O(n).

Why O(n) beats O(n log n): frequency map comparison is O(1) for fixed alphabet. Sorting each string is O(k log k) per string. For large inputs or many strings, the frequency map approach is significantly faster.
lessons.analogy: A character frequency map is a fingerprint. Two people can look completely different (different word order) yet have identical fingerprints (same character frequencies) — they are anagrams. Checking whether two people match by fingerprint comparison is instant (O(1) for fixed alphabet). Finding everyone in a crowd with a specific fingerprint means checking each person once — O(n) with a sliding window.

visual_explanation.description: Draw three strings: 'eat', 'tea', 'tan'. Below each, draw a 26-slot bar chart showing character frequencies. 'eat' and 'tea' have identical bar charts (e=1, a=1, t=1, all others 0) — they are anagrams. 'tan' has a different chart (t=1, a=1, n=1) — not an anagram of the others. Draw an arrow from 'eat' and 'tea' both pointing to the same sorted key 'aet'. Draw 'tan' pointing to its own key 'ant'. Label: 'Same sorted key = same group = anagrams'.

code_example.explanation: In findAnagrams, comparing two 26-element arrays with .join() is O(26) = O(1) per comparison. The sliding window does n - p.length + 1 comparisons total. Overall: O(n). A more optimised version tracks a 'matches' counter to avoid the array comparison entirely, reducing the constant factor.

common_mistakes: Sorting strings to check anagrams when a frequency map is available — sorting is O(n log n) and unnecessary when frequency array comparison is O(1). Know when each approach is better based on context
Not handling strings with characters outside a-z — using a fixed 26-element array fails silently on uppercase, digits, or Unicode. Use a Map for general character sets
Rebuilding the frequency map from scratch at each window position — this makes the sliding window O(n × k) instead of O(n). Always update incrementally

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Group Anagrams. The candidate used sorted strings as keys (correct). The interviewer asked 'What is the complexity?' The candidate said 'O(n × k) where n is the number of strings and k is the average string length.' The interviewer said 'Does sorting factor into this?' Pause. The candidate corrected: 'O(n × k log k) — each sort is O(k log k) and we sort n strings.' The interviewer then asked 'Can you do better?' The candidate thought for 30 seconds and said 'Yes — use a frequency tuple as the key instead of sorting. Building the frequency array is O(k) not O(k log k), reducing total to O(n × k).' That answer got the hire.
interview_war_story.lesson: Knowing the correct answer is the baseline. Being able to derive a better answer from first principles when prompted is what differentiates strong candidates.

lessons.interview_relevance: Group Anagrams (#49), Valid Anagram (#242), and Find All Anagrams in a String (#438) are Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 problems tested directly. The pattern — frequency map as fingerprint, sliding window for substring matching — recurs across dozens of string problems.

questions.question: In isAnagram, why do we increment the count array for characters in s and decrement for characters in t, then check if all values are zero?
options: Because we need to check if both strings have the same total character count
Because incrementing for s and decrementing for t means anagrams will perfectly cancel to zero — any mismatch in frequency leaves a non-zero value
Because zeros are faster to check than comparing two separate arrays
This approach only works if both strings are the same length
questions.explanation: If s and t are anagrams, every character that appears in s also appears the same number of times in t. Incrementing for s and decrementing for t means each character's net count is 0 if frequencies match. Any character that appears more in s than t leaves a positive value; more in t than s leaves a negative value. All-zeros confirms identical frequencies.

questions.question: Group Anagrams uses sorted strings as keys (O(k log k) per string). What is a faster approach and what is its complexity?
options: Use the string length as the key — O(1) per string
Use a frequency tuple as the key (e.g. '1_0_0_1_0_...') — building the frequency array is O(k) not O(k log k), reducing total from O(n×k log k) to O(n×k)
Sort the entire input first — O(n log n) total
No faster approach exists — O(k log k) per string is optimal
questions.explanation: Building a 26-element frequency array for a string of length k is O(k). Converting it to a key string like '1_0_0_1...' is O(26) = O(1). Total: O(n × k) instead of O(n × k log k). At large inputs with long strings, this is a meaningful improvement.

questions.question: In findAnagrams (sliding window on 'cbaebabacd' with p='abc'), how do you update the window frequency array as the window slides one step right?
options: Rebuild the entire frequency array for the new window position
Add the new right character (increment its count) and remove the old left character (decrement its count) — O(1) update per step
Clear the array and scan the new window from scratch
Sort the new window and compare with sorted p
questions.explanation: The incremental update is the key insight: wCount[s[right]]++ and wCount[s[right-len(p)]]--. This is O(1) per step. Rebuilding from scratch would be O(k) per step, making the total O(n×k) instead of O(n).

Write the O(n×k) brute force (rebuild frequency map at each position), then the O(n) sliding window solution that updates the map incrementally.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: The brute force shown is correct but O(n×k). For s of length 100,000 and p of length 1,000, this is 100,000,000 operations. The sliding window reduces this to 200,000 operations (2n) by maintaining the frequency array incrementally instead of rebuilding it.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n×k) time — multiplied inner scan at each window position

optimal_solution.complexity: O(n) time — each character visited once, O(1) window update per step. O(1) space — fixed 26-element arrays.

test_cases.label: Classic example: anagrams at positions 0 and 6

hints.text: Build pCount and the first window's wCount in the same loop over p.length characters. After that, check if they match. Then slide: for each new right position, add s[right] to wCount and remove s[right - p.length] from wCount.

wCount[s.charCodeAt(right) - 97]++ adds the new right character. wCount[s.charCodeAt(right - p.length) - 97]-- removes the character that just left the window's left side. After both updates, compare pCount.join() === wCount.join().
In the slide loop: wCount[s.charCodeAt(right) - 97]++; wCount[s.charCodeAt(right - p.length) - 97]--; if (pCount.join() === wCount.join()) result.push(right - p.length + 1);

theory_mcq.question: Why does `isAnagram` use a single 26-element array, incrementing for one string and decrementing for the other, rather than two separate frequency maps?
options: It is purely a stylistic preference with no efficiency benefit

Using one shared array and incrementing/decrementing means that if both strings have IDENTICAL character frequencies, every count returns to exactly 0 — a single, simple final check (`count.every(c => c === 0)`) confirms the anagram relationship without needing to compare two separate arrays element-by-element
It uses less memory than any other possible approach
Two separate frequency maps would produce incorrect results
theory_mcq.explanation: This is an elegant simplification: by incrementing for string s and decrementing for string t on the SAME array, matching frequencies cancel out to zero. If they're true anagrams, every position ends at 0; if not, at least one position will be nonzero, both checked with one simple .every() call instead of comparing two separate arrays.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson note 'Character map vs sorting: O(n) vs O(n log n)' as a meaningful comparison for anagram detection?
options: Sorting and character maps always have identical complexity

Sorting both strings and comparing them (an alternative anagram-detection approach) costs O(n log n) due to the sort step, while a character-frequency-array approach (fixed 26-element alphabet) achieves O(n) — a real, meaningful complexity improvement when frequent anagram checks matter
Sorting is always faster than character maps
This distinction only matters for strings longer than 1 million characters
theory_mcq.explanation: An alternative correct approach (sort each string and compare) costs O(n log n) due to the sorting step. The character-frequency-array approach in this lesson achieves a strictly better O(n), since it relies on a single linear pass with O(1) array indexing rather than a comparison-based sort.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `isAnagram('rat', 'car')`. What happens to count[r-97] (the index for 'r'), and what does this reveal about the final result?
options: count[r-97] ends at 0, same as all other indices

count[r-97] is incremented once (from 'rat') but never decremented (since 'car' contains no 'r'), leaving it at +1 — this nonzero value means count.every(c => c === 0) returns false, correctly identifying 'rat' and 'car' as NOT anagrams
count[r-97] is decremented to -1
The function throws an error for this input
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's stated result: 'rat' increments r's count, but 'car' (r,a,c... wait, car has no 'r') never decrements it back, leaving count[r-97]=+1, which is nonzero — correctly signaling that these strings are not anagrams since their character sets differ.

logic_mcq.question: In `groupAnagrams(['eat','tea','tan','ate','nat','bat'])`, why do 'eat', 'tea', and 'ate' all map to the same key, while 'tan' and 'nat' map to a different shared key?
options: Because all six strings happen to be the same length

Because sorting each string's characters alphabetically produces a canonical 'fingerprint' — 'eat','tea','ate' all sort to 'aet', while 'tan' and 'nat' both sort to 'ant' — so anagrams of each other always produce the identical sorted-key, grouping them together in the Map regardless of original character order
Because the Map randomly assigns keys
Because 'eat', 'tea', and 'ate' are not actually anagrams
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's exact worked example: sorting each string's characters produces a canonical representation that's identical for all anagrams of each other ('eat'->'aet', 'tea'->'aet', 'ate'->'aet'), which is precisely why the sorted string works as a grouping key in the Map.

logic_mcq.question: In `findAnagrams('cbaebabacd', 'abc')`, the result is `[0, 6]`. What does each of these indices represent?
options: Random positions with no meaning

Index 0 means the substring starting at position 0 ('cba') is an anagram of 'abc'; index 6 means the substring starting at position 6 ('bac') is also an anagram of 'abc' — these are the starting positions of every length-3 substring of s that's an anagram of p
These indices represent the length of the string
Both indices represent the same substring counted twice
logic_mcq.explanation: findAnagrams returns the STARTING indices of every substring in s with the same length as p that is a character-frequency match (anagram) of p — here, s[0:3]='cba' and s[6:9]='bac' are both rearrangements of 'abc', matching the function's stated result.

syntax_mcq.question: In `pCount.join() === wCount.join()`, why does comparing the joined string representations work as a way to check if two frequency arrays are equal?
options: This comparison is actually incorrect and will give wrong results

`.join()` converts each array into a comma-separated string (e.g., [2,0,1] -> '2,0,1'); two arrays produce IDENTICAL joined strings if and only if they have the same elements in the same positions, so comparing the joined strings is a correct (if not maximally efficient) way to check array equality
join() sorts the array before converting to a string
This only works for arrays containing strings, not numbers
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.join()` with no separator argument defaults to a comma, converting the array into a deterministic string representation. Since two equal arrays produce identical strings, comparing the join() results is a valid (though not the most performant) way to check array equality position-by-position.

lessons.title: Subarray Problems
lessons.objective: Recognise and solve the five canonical subarray problem types using the correct pattern for each, reducing O(n²) or O(n³) brute forces to O(n) optimal solutions.
concepts: Maximum subarray sum: Kadane's algorithm O(n)
Subarray with target sum: prefix sum + hash map O(n)
Minimum size subarray sum: sliding window O(n)
Maximum product subarray: track both max and min O(n)
Subarray pattern recognition signals
When to use Kadane's vs sliding window vs prefix sum
Brute force O(n²) baseline for each type
lessons.explanation:
Subarray problems are among the most frequently tested array problems. Each variant has a canonical optimal algorithm.

Kadane's Algorithm (max subarray sum): at each element, decide whether to extend the current subarray or start fresh. currentSum = max(num, currentSum + num). If currentSum + num < num alone, the current subarray is a burden — cut it and start fresh at num. Track the global maximum throughout.

Prefix Sum + Hash Map (subarray sum equals k): for each prefix sum, check if (prefixSum - k) was seen before. Each such occurrence corresponds to a valid subarray. Works even with negative numbers — sliding window does not.

Sliding Window (min size with target sum, POSITIVE integers only): expand right, shrink left when sum ≥ target, track minimum window size. Requires positive integers for monotonicity.

Max Product Subarray: track both the maximum AND minimum product ending at each position, because a very negative minimum times a negative new element becomes the new maximum.
lessons.analogy: Kadane's algorithm is like a traveller counting the net value collected on their journey. At each city, they decide: is it worth continuing from where I am (currentSum + num), or should I cut ties and start fresh in this city (num alone)? If the journey so far has been a net burden, cut it. The global maximum is the best journey segment ever seen.

visual_explanation.description: Draw the array [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]. Below it, draw two rows: 'currentSum' and 'maxSum' after processing each element. Show: currentSum = -2, 1, -2, 4, 3, 5, 6, 1, 5. maxSum = -2, 1, 1, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 6. Highlight the reset moments: after index 0 (currentSum goes from -2 to 1 when the algorithm chooses to start fresh at 1). Draw a bracket under elements [4,-1,2,1] labelled 'optimal subarray = 6'. Mark each max(num, currentSum+num) decision explicitly.

code_example.explanation: Tracking both max and min product is the key insight of the product variant. A very negative min product becomes a very positive max product when multiplied by a negative number. This is why Kadane's algorithm cannot be directly applied — the minimum must be preserved as a potential future maximum.

common_mistakes: Initialising currentSum to 0 in Kadane's instead of nums[0] — a zero initialisation returns 0 when all elements are negative, but the correct answer is the least negative element (e.g., [-3,-2,-1] should return -1, not 0)

Using sliding window for subarray sum with negative numbers — sliding window requires the invariant that adding elements increases the sum. Negative numbers break this, so prefix sum + hash map is the correct tool
Forgetting to track the minimum product in the product variant — skipping the minimum means missing the case where two negatives multiply to produce a new maximum

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Maximum Subarray. The candidate wrote Kadane's correctly. The interviewer asked 'What if I initialised currentSum to 0 instead of nums[0]?' The candidate thought and said 'For positive-only arrays, it would still work. But for all-negative arrays like [-5, -3, -1], your version would return 0 — no subarray exists that sums to 0, so 0 is incorrect. My initialisation to nums[0] guarantees the answer is always an actual subarray element, even in the all-negative case.' The interviewer wrote 'hire'. The candidate who initialised to 0 and could not explain why would have been a no-hire.
interview_war_story.lesson: Every initialisation decision in an algorithm should be explainable. 'Why nums[0] and not 0?' is the follow-up that reveals whether you understood Kadane's or just memorised it.

lessons.interview_relevance: Maximum Subarray (#53) is one of the most frequently asked Blind 75 problems. Kadane's algorithm is expected knowledge. Product Variant (#152), Subarray Sum Equals K (#560), and Minimum Size Subarray Sum (#209) are all NeetCode 150. Selecting the correct algorithm variant on first read is the target skill.

questions.question: In Kadane's algorithm, why must currentSum be initialised to nums[0] and not 0?
options: Because nums[0] is always the correct answer
Because initialising to 0 returns 0 for all-negative arrays — but the correct answer is the least negative element (an actual subarray), not 0 which represents an empty subarray
Because the algorithm requires starting from the first element
There is no difference — both initialisations give the same result
questions.explanation: For all-negative arrays like [-5, -3, -1], the correct answer is -1 (the single least negative element). Initialising currentSum to 0 would give maxSum = 0 — implying an empty subarray with sum 0 exists, which is wrong. Initialising to nums[0] ensures the result is always an actual subarray.

questions.question: An array contains both positive and negative integers. You need to count subarrays with sum exactly k. Why can't you use sliding window for this?
options: Sliding window only works for strings, not arrays

Sliding window requires the invariant that adding elements to the right increases the window sum. Negative numbers break this — you might need to add a negative element to reach target k, or shrinking from the left might increase the sum.
Sliding window is O(n²) and too slow
Sliding window cannot count — it only finds the longest/shortest
questions.explanation: Sliding window works when adding elements to the right monotonically increases the aggregate (sum, product, etc.) and removing from the left decreases it. Negative numbers break this monotonicity — a negative element might decrease the sum when added on the right, making it impossible to know when to shrink from the left. Use prefix sum + hash map instead.

questions.question: In the maximum product subarray problem, array is [-2, 3, -4]. Trace: what is the maximum product?
options: 3 (single element -2 has product 2, 3 has product 3, single -4 has product -4)
24 (the full array: -2 × 3 × -4 = 24)
-2 (the first element)
12 (3 × -4 = -12, take absolute value)
questions.explanation: -2 × 3 × -4 = 24. The tracking: start maxProd=-2, minProd=-2. At 3: candidates=[3, -6, -6] → maxProd=3, minProd=-6. At -4: candidates=[-4, -12, 24] → maxProd=24, minProd=-12. Result=24. The minimum product at position 2 (-6) became the maximum when multiplied by -4.

coding_quest.title: Kadane's Algorithm With Subarray Tracking
coding_quest.problem_statement: Implement Kadane's algorithm to find the maximum subarray sum. Then extend it to also return the start and end indices of that maximum subarray. Finally, add handling for the all-negative edge case to ensure the answer is always an actual subarray element, not 0.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: The wrong initialisation is currentSum = 0, maxSum = 0. This gives 0 for all-negative arrays — implying an empty subarray exists with sum 0. But the problem asks for the maximum subarray of at least one element. The correct initialisation is currentSum = maxSum = nums[0].
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: Logically incorrect for all-negative arrays — returns 0 instead of the least negative element

hints.text: For Part 1: initialise currentSum = nums[0] and maxSum = nums[0]. Then loop from i=1. At each step: currentSum = Math.max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i]). If currentSum > maxSum, update maxSum.

For Part 2: maintain tempStart as the starting index of the current subarray. When you choose to start fresh (nums[i] > currentSum + nums[i]), set tempStart = i. When you update maxSum (currentSum > maxSum), copy tempStart to start and set end = i.

For Part 2 inside the loop: if (nums[i] > currentSum + nums[i]) { currentSum = nums[i]; tempStart = i; } else { currentSum += nums[i]; } if (currentSum > maxSum) { maxSum = currentSum; start = tempStart; end = i; }

lessons.mini_challenge: Given [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4], trace Kadane's algorithm step by step: write the value of currentSum and maxSum after processing each element. Verify the answer is 6. Then identify the start and end indices of the maximum subarray.

theory_mcq.question: What is the core insight behind Kadane's Algorithm that allows it to find the maximum subarray sum in O(n) time?
options: It checks every possible subarray individually but very quickly

At each position, the algorithm decides whether to EXTEND the current subarray (if doing so increases the sum) or START FRESH from the current element (if the accumulated sum has become a net negative drag) — this local greedy decision, made once per element, provably leads to the global maximum without needing to examine every subarray explicitly
It only works on arrays containing exclusively positive numbers
It sorts the array first, then sums the largest elements
theory_mcq.explanation: Kadane's core insight, shown in `currentSum = Math.max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i])`: at each step, decide whether the running sum so far is still helping (extend) or has become a net negative (start fresh at the current element) — this single O(1) decision per element, repeated n times, finds the global maximum in O(n) total.

theory_mcq.question: Why must `maxProduct` track BOTH a running maximum AND a running minimum product, unlike Kadane's sum version which only needs a running maximum?
options: Tracking the minimum is unnecessary; this is an error in the lesson

Because multiplying by a NEGATIVE number can flip a very negative (small) product into a very positive (large) one — so the current minimum product is a candidate for becoming the NEW maximum if the next number is negative, which sum-based Kadane's doesn't need to worry about since addition doesn't have this sign-flipping property
Because product calculations are always twice as expensive as sum calculations
Because arrays with products always have exactly two valid answers
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's key distinguishing insight for the product variant: unlike addition, multiplication by a negative number can turn the smallest (most negative) running product into the largest (most positive) one — so you must track both extremes at every step, since either could become the new maximum depending on the sign of the next number.

logic_mcq.question: Trace Kadane's algorithm on `[-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4]`. According to the lesson's trace, what is the final answer, and which subarray produces it?
options: Answer: 6, from subarray [4,-1,2,1]
Answer: -2, from the first element alone
Answer: 15, the sum of all positive numbers
Answer: 4, from the single element 4
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's own worked trace, with maxSum reaching 6 at the point where currentSum accumulates through [4,-1,2,1] = 4-1+2+1 = 6, which is indeed the maximum subarray sum for this input as explicitly stated in the lesson.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `maxProduct([-2,3,-4])`. Why does the result end up being 24 (the product of ALL elements), rather than just 3 (the largest single positive number)?
options: This is incorrect; the actual answer should be 3

Because the two negative numbers (-2 and -4) multiply together to produce a positive 8, and combined with 3, the full-array product -2×3×-4=24 is larger than any partial product — this is exactly the scenario the min-tracking logic is designed to catch, since a running minimum (very negative) can become the new maximum once multiplied by another negative
Because the algorithm always returns the product of the entire array regardless of values
Because 24 is simply incorrect output from a buggy algorithm
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's stated result exactly: two negatives multiplying to a positive means the FULL array's product (24) beats any subset, and this is precisely why tracking the running minimum (which captures the most-negative running product) is essential — it can flip to become the new maximum when multiplied by a subsequent negative number.

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's pattern selection guide, a problem asking for 'the minimum SIZE subarray with sum at least target, given all POSITIVE numbers' should use which technique?
options: Kadane's algorithm

Sliding window — since the constraint mentions a size requirement on a contiguous subarray with positive numbers (meaning the window sum changes monotonically as it expands/shrinks), matching the lesson's explicit recognition signal: 'Min SIZE with sum >= target, POSITIVE -> sliding window O(n)'
Prefix sum + hashmap
Matrix traversal
logic_mcq.explanation: This exactly matches the lesson's stated pattern selection guide entry: 'Min SIZE with sum >= target, POSITIVE numbers -> sliding window O(n)' — the all-positive constraint is what makes the window's sum behave monotonically, enabling the sliding window technique to work correctly.

syntax_mcq.question: In `const candidates = [num, maxProd * num, minProd * num]; maxProd = Math.max(...candidates);`, what does the spread operator `...` accomplish?
options: It creates a copy of the candidates array without changing anything

It expands the array `candidates` into individual arguments, so `Math.max(...candidates)` is equivalent to `Math.max(candidates[0], candidates[1], candidates[2])` — necessary because Math.max expects individual number arguments, not an array
It deletes the candidates array after use
It converts the array to a string
syntax_mcq.explanation: `Math.max()` doesn't accept an array directly — it expects comma-separated arguments. The spread operator `...candidates` unpacks the array's elements as individual arguments, allowing `Math.max(...candidates)` to correctly find the maximum among all three candidate values.

coding_challenges.title: Subarray Pattern Selector and Solver
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement Kadane's algorithm for maximum subarray sum, the max-product variant, and a minimum-size-subarray-sum sliding window solution, then build a simple pattern selector function that picks the right approach based on a problem descriptor.
requirements: Implement `maxSubArraySum(nums)` using Kadane's algorithm exactly as in the lesson
Implement `maxProductSubarray(nums)` tracking both max and min running products
Implement `minSubArrayLen(target, nums)` using sliding window to find the minimum length subarray (all positive numbers) with sum >= target, returning 0 if no such subarray exists

Implement `selectPattern(descriptor)` that returns the correct pattern name string based on the lesson's recognition signals: descriptors 'max_sum', 'max_product', 'min_size_sum_positive' map to 'Kadane', 'Kadane variant (min tracking)', 'Sliding Window' respectively
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: maxSubArraySum: O(n) time, O(1) space. maxProductSubarray: O(n) time, O(1) space. minSubArrayLen: O(n) time, O(1) space (sliding window, amortized — left pointer moves at most n times total across the whole run).

hints.text: maxSubArraySum: at each step, currentSum is either the current element alone, or the current element added to the previous currentSum, whichever is larger.
maxProductSubarray: at each step, compute all three candidates (current number alone, max*current, min*current), then take the max and min of those three as the new running max/min.
minSubArrayLen: expand the window by adding nums[right]; whenever sum >= target, record the window length and shrink from the left while still valid.

lessons.title: Matrix Traversal Basics
lessons.objective: Traverse 2D matrices using row-major and column-major order, apply directional traversal for neighbour-based problems, and implement spiral and in-place rotation patterns.
concepts: 2D array representation and index arithmetic: matrix[row][col]
Row-major traversal: O(m×n) with good cache locality
Column-major traversal and why it is slower in practice
Four-directional neighbour traversal with bounds checking
Spiral order traversal: four shrinking boundaries
In-place matrix rotation 90 degrees: transpose then reverse rows
Set zero problem: propagation traps and the O(1) space solution
lessons.explanation:
A matrix is a 2D array accessed as matrix[row][col]. Row-major traversal (outer loop over rows, inner loop over columns) accesses memory sequentially in JavaScript, benefiting from cache locality. Column-major traversal jumps between rows in memory, causing more cache misses.

For neighbour problems (flood fill, number of islands, game of life), define a directions array: [[0,1],[0,-1],[1,0],[-1,0]] representing right, left, down, up. For each cell, iterate over directions, compute neighbour coordinates, and bounds-check before accessing.

Spiral traversal maintains four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) that shrink inward after each pass.

In-place 90-degree clockwise rotation: first transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), then reverse each row. Both operations are O(n²) time and O(1) space — no extra matrix needed.
lessons.analogy: Traversing a matrix is like reading a printed grid. Row-major is reading left-to-right, top-to-bottom — the natural order. Column-major is reading top-to-bottom in each column — against the natural page flow, slower and more disorienting. Spiral order is reading from the outer border inward, like peeling layers from a square onion. Each layer reveals another layer underneath until you reach the centre.

visual_explanation.description: Draw a 4×4 matrix with numbers. Show three separate traversal paths with numbered arrows: (1) Row-major: left-to-right, top-to-bottom, numbered 1-16 in reading order. (2) Spiral: start top-left, go right along top row, down right column, left along bottom row, up left column, then peel inward. Number each cell in spiral visit order. (3) Directions diagram: show a single cell with four arrows labelled [0,1]=right, [0,-1]=left, [1,0]=down, [-1,0]=up, and red X marks on arrows that go out of bounds. Show the bounds check formula: r >= 0 && r < m && c >= 0 && c < n.

code_example.explanation: The DIRS array pattern (directional offsets with bounds checking) is used in every grid-based DFS and BFS problem in Module 10 and Level 2. Learning it here means it is muscle memory by the time you need it for Number of Islands, Flood Fill, and Course Schedule.

common_mistakes: Accessing matrix[row][col] without bounds checking — out-of-bounds access returns undefined in JavaScript instead of throwing, producing silently wrong results that are hard to debug
Forgetting the inner boundary guards in spiral traversal — when the matrix has an odd dimension, the centre row or column gets processed twice without the top <= bottom and left <= right guards
Rotating a matrix by creating a new matrix instead of in-place — the transpose-then-reverse pattern achieves O(1) extra space. Creating a new matrix uses O(n²) space unnecessarily

interview_war_story.story: The problem was to rotate a matrix 90 degrees. The candidate created a new n×n matrix and filled it with the rotated values — correct but O(n²) space. The interviewer said 'Can you do it in-place, O(1) space?' The candidate did not know the transpose-then-reverse trick. The interviewer gave a hint: 'Think about what a 90-degree rotation does to position (i,j) — where does it end up?' The candidate worked out: position (i,j) goes to (j, n-1-i). They then realised: transpose maps (i,j) to (j,i), and reversing rows maps (j,i) to (j, n-1-i). Together: the rotation. They coded it from the insight. The interviewer was satisfied — they wanted to see the candidate derive the algorithm from first principles, not recall a memorised procedure.
interview_war_story.lesson: If you blank on the trick, fall back to first principles: figure out where each element goes after rotation, then find a sequence of simple operations that achieves that mapping. Transpose then reverse is derivable from that analysis.

lessons.interview_relevance: Spiral Order (#54), Rotate Image (#48), and Set Matrix Zeroes (#73) are NeetCode 150 matrix problems. The four-directional neighbour traversal pattern is the direct prerequisite for Number of Islands (#200) and the flood fill family of DFS/BFS grid problems.

questions.question: What are the two steps to rotate an n×n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place with O(1) extra space?
options: Reverse each row, then reverse the entire matrix vertically
First transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), then reverse each row
First reverse each row, then transpose
Sort each row, then sort each column
questions.explanation: Transpose: swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for all i<j. This flips the matrix along its main diagonal. Then reverse each row. Together, these two operations achieve a 90-degree clockwise rotation. The order matters — reverse then transpose gives a counter-clockwise rotation instead.

questions.question: Why must you always bounds-check before accessing a matrix neighbour in JavaScript?
options: JavaScript arrays are slower without bounds checking
Without bounds checking, accessing matrix[-1][0] or matrix[m][0] returns undefined instead of throwing — producing silently wrong results that look like correct values
Matrix access is always O(n) without bounds checking
Bounds checking is only needed for very large matrices
questions.explanation: JavaScript does not throw for out-of-bounds array access. matrix[-1] returns undefined, and undefined[0] throws a TypeError — but only sometimes. matrix[m] (one past the end) returns undefined, and checking undefined[0] might return undefined silently. Always check r >= 0 && r < m && c >= 0 && c < n before accessing.

questions.question: In spiral traversal of a matrix, why are the guards (top <= bottom) and (left <= right) needed before processing the bottom row and left column?
options: To avoid going out of bounds

To handle matrices where after processing the top row and right column, the top boundary has crossed bottom or left has crossed right — meaning we are at the centre of an odd-dimension matrix and the centre row/column would be processed twice without the guard
To improve performance
These guards are only needed for square matrices
questions.explanation: For a 3×3 matrix, after processing the top row (top++), right column (right--), the inner top might equal bottom (both at the centre row). Without the guard, we would process the centre row twice — once as the top row (already done) and once as the bottom row. The guard prevents this double-processing.

coding_quest.title: Spiral Order Matrix Traversal
coding_quest.problem_statement: Given an m×n matrix, return all elements in spiral order (clockwise from top-left, layer by layer inward). Apply the 5-step framework. Use the four-boundary approach (top, bottom, left, right) that shrinks after each directional pass. Include the inner boundary guards.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: The common wrong approach is missing the inner boundary guards for the bottom row and left column. Without them, a 3×3 matrix processes the centre row twice — once as the top row after the first shrink, and once as the bottom row before the second shrink. The guard if (top <= bottom) before the bottom row ensures this cannot happen.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: Produces wrong output for matrices with odd dimensions — processes the centre row/col twice

optimal_solution.complexity: O(m×n) time — each element visited exactly once. O(1) extra space — only boundary variables.

hints.text: Initialise four boundaries: top=0, bottom=rows-1, left=0, right=cols-1. In each while iteration: traverse top row (left→right), then right col (top→bottom), then bottom row (right→left, GUARDED by top<=bottom), then left col (bottom→top, GUARDED by left<=right). Shrink the boundary after each pass.

Top row: for (let c = left; c <= right; c++) result.push(matrix[top][c]); then top++. Right col: for (let r = top; r <= bottom; r++) result.push(matrix[r][right]); then right--. Bottom row: if (top <= bottom) for (let c = right; c >= left; c--) result.push(matrix[bottom][c]); then bottom--.

Left col: if (left <= right) for (let r = bottom; r >= top; r--) result.push(matrix[r][left]); then left++. The two if guards prevent the centre element from being added twice in odd-dimension matrices.

lessons.mini_challenge: Implement Set Matrix Zeroes: given an m×n matrix, if any element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0 in-place. Implement the O(1) space version that uses the first row and first column of the matrix itself as markers. Explain why you must process the first row and column last.

theory_mcq.question: Why does row-major traversal have 'good cache locality' while column-major traversal is described as slower in practice, even though both are O(m×n)?
options: Cache locality has no real performance impact

Row-major traversal accesses elements that are contiguous in memory (since 2D arrays are typically stored row-by-row internally), which the CPU's cache can prefetch efficiently; column-major traversal jumps across rows for each step, accessing memory locations far apart, causing more cache misses despite doing the same total NUMBER of operations
Column-major traversal does strictly more operations than row-major
This distinction only applies to matrices larger than 1000x1000
theory_mcq.explanation: Both traversal orders are O(m×n) in raw operation count, but row-major traversal matches how 2D arrays are typically laid out in memory (row-by-row), giving good cache locality (sequential access). Column-major traversal accesses memory in a scattered pattern, causing more cache misses — same Big O, but meaningfully different real-world performance due to memory access patterns.

theory_mcq.question: Why is bounds checking (`r >= 0 && r < m && c >= 0 && c < n`) always necessary when computing a neighbor's position in a matrix?
options: Bounds checking is optional and only a defensive best practice

Without bounds checking, computing a neighbor at the edge or corner of the matrix (e.g., row=0 checking 'up') would produce an out-of-bounds index, which could cause incorrect behavior or runtime errors — checking ensures only valid, in-grid positions are considered
Bounds checking only matters for square matrices
JavaScript automatically prevents all out-of-bounds access
theory_mcq.explanation: Edge and corner cells have fewer than 4 valid neighbors (e.g., the top-left corner has only 2: right and down). Without explicit bounds checking, the directional offset calculation would compute invalid row/column indices for non-existent neighbors, which must be filtered out before use.

logic_mcq.question: Using `DIRS = [[0,1],[0,-1],[1,0],[-1,0]]` (right, left, down, up), what are the valid neighbors of position (0, 0) in a 3x3 matrix?
options: All four directions are valid: (0,1), (0,-1), (1,0), (-1,0)
Only 2 directions are valid: (0,1) [right] and (1,0) [down] — since (0,-1) [left] and (-1,0) [up] would both produce a negative index, which fails the bounds check (r >= 0 && c >= 0)
Only 1 direction is valid
No directions are valid from the corner
logic_mcq.explanation: From (0,0), moving left would give column -1 (invalid) and moving up would give row -1 (invalid) — both fail the `>= 0` bounds check. Only right (0,1) and down (1,0) produce valid, in-bounds positions, confirming that corner cells have exactly 2 neighbors in this 4-directional scheme.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `spiralOrder` on a 3x3 matrix [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]. What is the resulting order, following the lesson's top-right-bottom-left pattern?
options: 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 (simple row-major order)
1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5 — top row left-to-right, then right column top-to-bottom, then bottom row right-to-left, then left column bottom-to-top, then the remaining center element
1,4,7,2,5,8,3,6,9 (column-major order)
logic_mcq.explanation: Tracing the spiral: top row (1,2,3) left-to-right, then right column (6,9) top-to-bottom (skipping 3, already visited), then bottom row (8,7) right-to-left (skipping 9), then left column (4) bottom-to-top (skipping 7), then the center (5) remains — giving 1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5, matching the standard spiral traversal pattern this lesson implements.

logic_mcq.question: In the in-place rotation function, why does the algorithm perform a TRANSPOSE first, then REVERSE each row, rather than directly computing each element's final rotated position?
options: This two-step approach is unnecessarily complicated and a single-step approach doesn't exist

Transpose-then-reverse-rows is a well-known decomposition that achieves a 90-degree clockwise rotation using only simple, easy-to-verify O(1)-space operations (swapping pairs across the diagonal, then reversing rows in place) — avoiding the need to allocate a separate output matrix or carefully derive a single complex index-mapping formula
This approach actually rotates the matrix 180 degrees, not 90
Transpose alone is sufficient; the row reversal step is redundant
logic_mcq.explanation: The transpose-then-reverse-rows technique is a standard, provably-correct decomposition: transposing swaps the matrix across its main diagonal, and then reversing each row completes the 90-degree clockwise rotation — both steps are simple in-place operations (O(1) extra space), avoiding the complexity of deriving and implementing a direct index-mapping formula for each element's final position.

syntax_mcq.question: In `for (const [dr, dc] of DIRS) { const r = row + dr, c = col + dc; ... }`, what does the destructuring `[dr, dc]` accomplish within the for-of loop?
options: It creates a new array on every iteration with no purpose

Since DIRS is an array of [rowDelta, colDelta] pairs, this destructures each pair directly into the named variables `dr` and `dc` during iteration, making the subsequent calculation `row + dr, col + dc` clear and readable without needing to index into each pair manually (e.g., avoiding `dir[0]`, `dir[1]`)
It filters out invalid directions automatically
It sorts the DIRS array before iterating
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is array destructuring applied within a for-of loop: each element of DIRS (itself a 2-element array like [0,1]) is unpacked directly into `dr` and `dc`, avoiding the need for manual indexing (`dir[0]`, `dir[1]`) and making the neighbor-offset calculation more readable.

syntax_mcq.question: What does `matrix[i].reverse()` do, called inside a loop over each row index `i`?
options: It reverses the entire matrix (all rows), not just one row
It reverses the elements WITHIN the i-th row in place (Array.prototype.reverse() mutates the array it's called on), which is the second step of the transpose-then-reverse 90-degree rotation technique
It deletes the i-th row entirely
It creates a new matrix without modifying the original
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.reverse()` is an in-place array method that reverses the order of elements within the array it's called on. Called as `matrix[i].reverse()`, it reverses just the i-th row's elements, which combined with the prior transpose step completes the 90-degree clockwise rotation.

coding_challenges.title: Matrix Traversal Toolkit
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement the core matrix traversal operations from this lesson: directional neighbor finding, spiral order traversal, and in-place 90-degree rotation, ensuring correct bounds-checking and in-place behavior where specified.
requirements: Implement `getNeighboursImpl(matrix, row, col)` using the 4-directional DIRS array with proper bounds checking
Implement `spiralOrderImpl(matrix)` matching the lesson's shrinking-boundary approach

Implement `rotateImpl(matrix)` performing an IN-PLACE 90-degree clockwise rotation via transpose-then-reverse-rows, modifying the input matrix directly (no return value needed, or return the same mutated matrix)
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: getNeighboursImpl: O(1) (fixed 4 directions checked). spiralOrderImpl: O(m×n) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output). rotateImpl: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space — purely in-place, no new matrix allocated.

hints.text: getNeighboursImpl: for each [dr,dc] in DIRS, compute the candidate position and check it's within [0, m) and [0, n).

spiralOrderImpl: maintain four shrinking boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and traverse top row, right column, bottom row, left column in sequence, with guards to avoid double-processing the center row/column.
rotateImpl: first swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for all j>i (transpose), then call .reverse() on each row.

lessons.title: Array Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Given any array or string problem, apply a structured decision process to select the correct pattern within 60 seconds — building the pattern-recognition reflex that makes all Module 2 techniques automatic.
concepts: Pattern selection decision tree for array and string problems
Recognition signals for each of the five patterns learned
Combining patterns: prefix sum + hash map, sliding window + frequency map
The standard playbook for reducing O(n²) to O(n)
When brute force is the intended solution (small n constraints)
Common traps: modifying array during traversal, off-by-one in windows
Building a personal problem catalogue
Module 2 review: 10 Blind 75 problems now solvable
lessons.explanation:
After learning five patterns in this module, the high-value skill is knowing which pattern to apply within 60 seconds of reading a problem.

The decision process:
1. What is the problem asking for? — maximum, minimum, count, specific subarray, substring
2. What is the structural constraint? — sorted array, positive-only, contiguous, pairs
3. Map to a pattern:
   - Pairs in a sorted array → Two Pointers
   - Contiguous subarray with sum/uniqueness constraint → Sliding Window
   - Multiple range queries or counting subarrays with target → Prefix Sum + Hash Map
   - Character frequency or anagram check → Character Map
   - Maximum subarray sum (negatives OK) → Kadane's

When a single pattern gives O(n²), look for a combination: Sliding Window + Set for uniqueness in O(n). Prefix Sum + Hash Map to count subarrays in O(n). These combinations are the intermediate-level problems that form the bulk of Blind 75.

Important: when the problem says n ≤ 100 or n ≤ 1000, the intended solution might be O(n²). Never over-optimise when the constraint makes brute force acceptable.
lessons.analogy: Pattern selection is like a doctor's differential diagnosis. The doctor does not run every test on every patient — they use presenting symptoms (problem constraints) to narrow to the most likely diagnosis (pattern), then apply the targeted treatment (algorithm). A doctor who runs every test on every patient will get the right answer eventually but will never complete a shift. Speed and accuracy come from systematic pattern matching, not exhaustive search.

visual_explanation.description: Draw a decision tree starting with 'Read the problem'. First branch: 'Contiguous subarray/substring?' YES → 'Fixed size k given?' YES → Fixed Sliding Window. NO → 'Need to count with target?' YES → Prefix Sum + Hash Map. NO → Variable Sliding Window. NO (not contiguous) → 'Sorted array + pairs?' YES → Two Pointers. → 'Character frequency?' YES → Character Map. → 'Max subarray sum?' YES → Kadane's. Add signal keywords next to each leaf node: 'longest/shortest' for variable window, 'exactly k' for fixed window, 'all anagrams' for character map.

code_example.explanation: count += right - left + 1 in a sliding window counts all valid subarrays ending at right: subarrays [left..right], [left+1..right], ..., [right..right]. There are exactly right - left + 1 of them. This counting trick appears in several NeetCode 150 problems and is worth memorising as a standalone pattern.

common_mistakes: Jumping to implementation before identifying the pattern — spending 30 minutes coding a brute force when the problem has an obvious sliding window signal is the most common time-wasting mistake

Treating every new problem as unique — there are no truly novel Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 problems. Every one is a variant of a known pattern. Train yourself to ask 'what pattern is this?' before anything else

Not building a personal problem catalogue — solving a problem, closing the tab, and moving on produces zero cumulative pattern recognition. Journal every problem with its pattern and re-solve it three days later

interview_war_story.story: The problem was: 'Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size exactly k.' The candidate immediately reached for Kadane's algorithm. After 5 minutes they had a solution, but it gave wrong answers. The interviewer said 'What is the constraint here?' The candidate re-read: 'exactly size k.' That is a fixed sliding window, not Kadane's. Kadane's finds the optimal subarray of any size. Fixed sliding window fixes the size to k. The candidate rewrote the solution in 3 minutes using a fixed window. The lesson: pattern recognition must come from careful reading of the problem constraint, not from the first keyword that pattern-matches.
interview_war_story.lesson: 'Maximum sum subarray' sounds like Kadane's. But 'maximum sum subarray of EXACTLY size k' is a fixed sliding window. One word changes the entire pattern. Always read the full constraint before selecting a pattern.

lessons.interview_relevance: The 10 Blind 75 problems listed above are directly solvable after this module. Solving all 10 from scratch, stating complexity, and explaining the pattern selection is the concrete outcome of Module 2. Schedule a timed session: 10 problems, 20 minutes each, 5-step framework applied to every one.

questions.question: A problem asks: 'Given a sorted array and a target, find two indices whose values sum to target.' Which pattern applies and why?
options: Sliding Window — contiguous subarray problem
Prefix Sum — involves summing elements
Two Pointers (opposite ends) — sorted array + pair + target sum is the canonical Two Pointer signal
Kadane's Algorithm — finding a maximum
questions.explanation: Sorted array + pair + target sum is the canonical Two Pointers (opposite ends) signal. Start with left=0, right=n-1. If sum < target: move left right. If sum > target: move right left. The sorted order guarantees the movement is always correct. This is exactly LeetCode #167 Two Sum II.

questions.question: A problem asks: 'Find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray of exactly size 3.' Which pattern is correct?
options: Kadane's Algorithm — maximum subarray sum
Variable Sliding Window — find the optimal window
Fixed Sliding Window — 'exactly size 3' means window size is fixed at k=3
Prefix Sum — sum of any range
questions.explanation: 'Exactly size k' = fixed sliding window. The window always contains exactly k elements — right and left move in lockstep, right always k steps ahead of left. Kadane's finds the optimal size — no fixed k. This is a common confusion point: 'maximum sum subarray' alone = Kadane's; 'maximum sum subarray of exactly size k' = fixed window.

questions.question: A problem states: 'An integer array may contain negatives. Count subarrays with sum exactly k.' Why is sliding window wrong here, and what is the correct pattern?
options: Sliding window is correct — all subarrays with a sum condition use sliding window
Sliding window fails because negative numbers break the monotonicity assumption — adding an element can decrease the sum. Use prefix sum + hash map instead: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Kadane's algorithm — count the maximum subarray
Two pointers — iterate from both ends
questions.explanation: Sliding window shrinks the left pointer when sum exceeds target — assuming adding elements increases the sum. Negative numbers break this: adding a negative decreases the sum, so you can never correctly decide when to shrink. Prefix sum + hash map works for any integers: at each position, check how many previous prefix sums equal (currentSum - k), each representing a valid subarray.

coding_quest.title: Pattern Decision: Best Time To Buy And Sell Stock
coding_quest.problem_statement: Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i, find the maximum profit you can achieve by buying on one day and selling on a later day. If no profit is possible, return 0. Apply the 5-step framework, identify the pattern (it is a Kadane's variant OR a greedy minimum-tracking approach — both are O(n)), and implement it. Do NOT use nested loops.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: The most common brute force is two nested loops: for each day i, scan all future days j and compute prices[j] - prices[i]. This is O(n²) and will time out for n=100,000. The key insight: you do not need to try every buy day. Just track the minimum price seen so far — that is always the best possible buy price for the current sell day.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n²) — will time out on LeetCode for n=100,000

optimal_solution.complexity: O(n) time | O(1) space — one pass, two variables

hints.text: At each day, the best profit if you sell today is prices[today] - (cheapest price seen before today). Track the cheapest price seen so far in a variable that updates as you scan left to right.

Initialise minPrice = prices[0] and maxProfit = 0. For each day from index 1: first update minPrice = Math.min(minPrice, prices[i]) (best buy price up to today), then update maxProfit = Math.max(maxProfit, prices[i] - minPrice) (best profit if selling today).
let minPrice = prices[0], maxProfit = 0; for (let i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) { minPrice = Math.min(minPrice, prices[i]); maxProfit = Math.max(maxProfit, prices[i] - minPrice); } return maxProfit;

theory_mcq.question: What is the purpose of the 'pattern selection decision tree' introduced in this lesson?
options: To memorize the solution to every specific LeetCode problem individually

To build a structured, reusable mapping from PROBLEM SIGNALS (phrases like 'sorted array + pair', 'longest contiguous + constraint', 'count subarrays with sum') to the CORRECT underlying pattern (Two Pointers, Sliding Window, Prefix Sum, etc.), enabling fast pattern recognition on NEW, previously unseen problems
To replace the need for understanding any individual pattern in depth
To only apply to problems explicitly labeled with their pattern name
theory_mcq.explanation: This lesson's explicit goal, consistent with L1-M01's broader philosophy, is building a transferable RECOGNITION skill: mapping problem language signals to underlying patterns, so unfamiliar problems can be solved by recognizing which of the ~5 techniques from this module applies, rather than requiring prior exposure to that exact problem.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson explicitly note 'when brute force is the intended solution (small n constraints)' as part of the decision process?
options: Brute force is never an acceptable interview answer

Sometimes the input size constraints given in a problem (e.g., n <= 20) are small enough that an O(n²) or even O(2^n) brute force is intentionally acceptable, and over-engineering an unnecessarily complex optimal solution wastes time when the simpler approach is both correct and sufficient for the given constraints
Brute force is always faster than any optimized pattern
This consideration only applies to string problems, never arrays
theory_mcq.explanation: Recognizing input size constraints is part of practical pattern selection: a problem explicitly bounding n to a small value (e.g., n <= 20) signals that an exponential or quadratic brute force is the EXPECTED solution, and reaching for unnecessary optimization in that case can waste interview time without adding value.

logic_mcq.question: A problem states: 'Given an array, find the longest contiguous subarray where the count of zeros is at most k.' Applying the lesson's decision tree, which pattern should be selected, and why?
options: Two Pointers (opposite ends), because the problem mentions an array

Variable Sliding Window, because the signal 'longest...contiguous' + 'at most k' (a constraint) exactly matches the lesson's stated recognition signal: 'longest/shortest contiguous + constraint -> VARIABLE SLIDING WINDOW'
Prefix Sum, because zeros need to be counted
Matrix Traversal, because the problem involves an array
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's own worked example (longestSubarrayKZeros): the phrase 'longest...contiguous' combined with the 'at most k' constraint directly matches the variable sliding window recognition signal, which is exactly the pattern the lesson's example function implements.

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's Blind 75 mapping, 'Product of Array Except Self' (id 238) is tagged with pattern 'Prefix Sum variant.' Based on what you know about prefix sums from L5, why might this specific problem be considered a VARIANT rather than a standard prefix sum application?
options: Because it has nothing to do with prefix sums at all

Because standard prefix sums (L5) compute running SUMS for range-sum queries, while this problem requires computing running PRODUCTS (prefix products from the left, and suffix products from the right, multiplied together per position) — the same underlying technique (precompute left-to-right, then combine with right-to-left) applied to a different operation than the sum-based examples in L5
Because it uses sliding window exclusively, with no relation to prefix sums
Because it can only be solved with Kadane's algorithm
logic_mcq.explanation: While L5 demonstrated prefix SUMS specifically, the underlying technique generalizes: precomputing a running aggregate from one direction (and often from the other direction too) to answer per-position queries efficiently is the same conceptual pattern applied here to PRODUCTS instead of sums, justifying its classification as a 'variant' of the prefix sum technique.

syntax_mcq.question: In `while (zeros > k) { if (nums[left++] === 0) zeros--; }`, what does the combined `nums[left++]` expression accomplish?
options: It only increments left without accessing the array

It reads the value at the CURRENT value of `left` (using it in the comparison `=== 0`), AND THEN increments `left` by one, all in a single expression — this is the post-increment operator combined with array access, advancing the window's left boundary while checking the value being removed
It is invalid JavaScript syntax
It deletes the element at index left
syntax_mcq.explanation: The post-increment operator `left++` returns the CURRENT value of `left` for use in the expression (here, as the array index), and only AFTER that increments the variable. So `nums[left++]` reads `nums[left]` first, then increments `left` — combining the 'check the value being removed from the window' and 'advance the left boundary' into one compact line.

coding_challenges.title: Capstone Project: Array Pattern Auto-Selector and Solver
coding_challenges.project_style: freeCodeCamp-style capstone project — synthesizes concepts from ALL 10 lessons in this module
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Build a tool that takes a structured problem descriptor (signals extracted from a problem statement) and both SELECTS the correct pattern AND solves a representative problem using that pattern, demonstrating mastery of all five core techniques from this module (Two Pointers, Sliding Window, Prefix Sum, Character Map, Kadane's) plus matrix traversal awareness.
requirements: Implement `detectPattern(signals)` taking an array of signal strings (e.g., ['sorted', 'pair_sum']) and returning the matching pattern name, using the lesson's recognition signal table (at minimum handle: sorted+pair->'Two Pointers', longest+constraint->'Sliding Window', range_sum_query->'Prefix Sum', anagram->'Character Map', max_subarray_sum->'Kadane')

Implement `solveWithDetectedPattern(problemType, input)` that calls detectPattern internally based on problemType, then dispatches to and returns the result of the appropriate solver function from this module's other challenges (you may reimplement minimal versions inline)

Implement `moduleSelfCheck()` returning an object summarizing which of the 5 core patterns have at least one working solver wired up, e.g. `{ twoPointers: true, slidingWindow: true, prefixSum: true, characterMap: true, kadane: true }`
Write a comment block documenting, in your own words, the recognition signal for EACH of the 5 patterns, mirroring this lesson's cheat sheet
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: detectPattern: O(1) (fixed-size signal checking). solveWithDetectedPattern dispatches to the underlying pattern's own complexity (e.g., O(n) for the two-pointer two-sum solver). This capstone demonstrates the META-skill of pattern selection itself, building on top of the concrete implementations from lessons 1-9.
